Case name: Manish Sisodia v. Central Bureau of Investigation
Issue in one line: Whether bail should be granted in linked corruption and PMLA cases given the evidence and likely trial length.
Holding in one line: Bail refused on the record then available; the Court preserved a fresh application if the trial failed to advance promptly.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India

Case name: Satyendar Kumar Jain v. Directorate of Enforcement
Issue in one line: Whether the accused met Section 45's twin bail requirements in alleged laundering through corporate entities.
Holding in one line: The appeals failed because the materials did not satisfy the statutory bail conditions; speedy-trial rights were nevertheless affirmed.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India

Case name: Tarsem Lal v. Directorate of Enforcement, Jalandhar Zonal Office
Issue in one line: Whether a PMLA accused not arrested before cognizance must apply for bail after appearing on summons, and how outstanding warrants should be treated.
Holding in one line: The appeals were allowed and warrants made cancellable on specified conditions; an accused appearing on summons need not seek bail, so anticipatory bail was unnecessary.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation

Case name: Manish Sisodia v. Directorate of Enforcement
Issue in one line: Whether continued custody without a timely trial justified granting bail on renewed applications.
Holding in one line: Both bail appeals were allowed because prolonged pretrial detention and slow progress outweighed continued incarceration on the facts.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Manish Sisodia v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2023)

Case name: Kalvakuntla Kavitha v. Directorate of Enforcement
Issue in one line: Whether a woman accused under the PMLA could be denied the statutory proviso solely because of her education or status.
Holding in one line: Bail was granted; the proviso for women could not be narrowed merely by describing the applicant as educated or influential.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Saumya Chaurasia v. Directorate of Enforcement

Case name: Prem Prakash v. Union of India through the Directorate of Enforcement
Issue in one line: Whether Section 50 statements and the other prima facie evidence satisfied Section 45 when determining regular bail in a land-transaction laundering case.
Holding in one line: The Court found the Section 45 twin conditions satisfied on the prima facie record, addressed the use of custody-obtained statements and ordered release on bail.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India

Case name: V. Senthil Balaji v. Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement
Issue in one line: Whether a lengthy likely trial and continuing incarceration warranted bail notwithstanding PMLA restrictions.
Holding in one line: The applicant was released on bail in view of extended custody and the absence of a realistic prospect of speedy completion of trial.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Manish Sisodia v. Directorate of Enforcement (2024)

Case name: Directorate of Enforcement v. Subhash Sharma
Issue in one line: Whether failure to produce a detained PMLA accused before a Magistrate within 24 hours vitiated arrest despite Section 45 bail restrictions.
Holding in one line: Dismissing the ED appeal, the Court upheld bail because unconstitutional detention violated Article 22(2), and Section 45 could not cure the unlawful arrest.

Case name: Union of India through Assistant Director v. Kanhaiya Prasad
Issue in one line: Whether the High Court could release a PMLA accused without addressing Section 45's mandatory conditions.
Holding in one line: The Court allowed the ED appeal, set aside the bail order for failure to apply Section 45, and directed surrender before fresh High Court consideration.
Precedent chiefly relied on: Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India

Issue in one line: Whether lack of trial progress after prolonged custody outweighed objections under Section 45.
Holding in one line: Bail was granted because 14 months of custody and examination of only one of 225 witnesses made early completion of trial unlikely under Article 21.
Precedent chiefly relied on: V. Senthil Balaji v. Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement

Case name: Mahesh Joshi v. Directorate of Enforcement
Issue in one line: Whether continued custody was justified where the older accused faced a document-heavy trial unlikely to finish within a reasonable time.
Holding in one line: Conditional bail was granted given over seven months of custody, 66 witnesses, extensive documents, the appellant’s age and the remote prospect of an early trial.
Precedent chiefly relied on: V. Senthil Balaji v. Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement

Case name: Arvind Dham v. Directorate of Enforcement
Issue in one line: Whether lengthy custody and an uncommenced, complex trial permitted release in a financial-crime prosecution.
Holding in one line: Bail was allowed because continued detention amid a large, uncommenced trial would undermine Article 21, notwithstanding the gravity of the alleged economic offences.
Precedent chiefly relied on: V. Senthil Balaji v. Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement
